chunks: Build an LPF or HPF with one inductor. The question: Build a LPF/HPF using a single inductor.
A filter needs a way to split a signal, and an inductor alone cannot do that. You pair it with one resistor.
The two form a divider: they share the input voltage, and the output is the share across one of them.
Put the inductor in series with the signal and you get a low-pass filter: slow signals pass, fast ones are blocked.
Put the inductor from the output to ground and you get a high-pass filter. Either way, one number sets the corner frequency.
Think of a water pipe with a heavy paddle wheel (the inductor) and a side drain. Slow, steady flow turns the wheel with little effort and gets through.
Rapid pulsing meets the wheel's resistance and gets stopped.
If you place the wheel in the side drain instead, steady flow slips out the side, and only rapid pulses are left going straight ahead.
The analogy is loose in one way: a real inductor also has wire resistance and stops working at very high frequency.
The same two components in swapped roles compared with the RC filters ("Build an LPF or HPF with one capacitor"): the inductor takes the place of the capacitor with the opposite filter type.
Both have f c = R/(2πL) = 15. 9 kilohertz for 1 kilohms and 10 millihenries.
Low-pass filter (LPF): passes frequencies below the corner. High-pass filter (HPF): passes frequencies above the corner.
Corner frequency: where the output has dropped to about 70% of its pass-band value, f c equals R over (2 pi L) .
Inductor impedance: the inductor's opposition to AC, 2 pi f L in size, which rises with frequency.
DCR: the wire resistance of a real inductor, which limits how well it blocks or shorts.
Say you want a low-pass filter with a corner at 15. 9 kilohertz into a 1 kilohms load.
Rearrange the formula: L equals R over (2 pi f c) equals 1000 over (2 pi times 15900) about 10 millihenries.
Place the 10 millihenries inductor in series with the signal, and the load resistor to ground. That is the whole idea.
"Inductor in series with the load is a low-pass; resistor in series with the inductor to ground is a high-pass. The corner is R over two pi L. For a 15.
9 kilohertz low-pass into 1 kilohm I need 10 millihenries. It's only practical at RF or on power lines, because at low frequency the inductors get huge.
And real inductors have DCR, which limits the high-pass stopband, and an SRF above which they stop working."
